# Chapter Index {#book-chapter-index .unnumbered}

This is the working architecture of the book. It is intentionally more detailed than a conventional table of contents: it records the question each chapter should answer and the subjects that belong there before prose is written. A linked title opens material already in the manuscript. Entries marked **Source draft** have early material retained in the repository, but are not linked into the book until that material is split and rewritten to match the approved structure.

## Part I - Understanding the execution problem

The reader first learns what an execution algorithm is trying to accomplish, how a market absorbs orders, and what it means to say that an execution was expensive.

### 1 [The Execution Problem](chapters/01-execution-problem.qmd#ch-control-lens) {#plan-1 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Frames execution as a decision problem in which inventory must be traded while prices, liquidity, and information continue to change. **Subtopics.** Parent and child orders; inventory dynamics and trading rate; market state, information, and admissible policies; implementation shortfall and terminal completion; immediacy, impact, price risk, and alpha decay; benchmarks and constraints; open-loop schedules and feedback policies; partial observation; Bellman recursion and the HJB equation; prediction, causal response, and control; model risk, units, and normalization.

### 2 [How Markets Absorb Orders](chapters/02-how-markets-absorb-orders.qmd#ch-microstructure) {#plan-2 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Builds an economic picture of the trading venue before reducing liquidity to a handful of model inputs. **Subtopics.** The bid, ask, spread, and depth; marketable and resting limit orders; price-time priority and queue position; book-walking cost; spread capture and adverse selection; fill and non-fill value; trade and order-flow imbalance; microprice; mechanical, informational, and common-cause price response; hidden liquidity and cancellations; replenishment and resilience; liquidity across horizons; calendar, event, and volume time; intraday seasonality; fragmentation and routing; dark liquidity; auctions; translating mechanism into control state.

### 3 [What Does an Execution Cost?](chapters/03-execution-cost.qmd#ch-tca) {#plan-3 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Defines the outcomes that execution research tries to explain and shows why the benchmark determines the economic question. **Subtopics.** Arrival-price implementation shortfall; VWAP, TWAP, close, and interval benchmarks; spread cost; timing risk; impact; opportunity cost; markouts; partial fills and unfinished orders; realized versus expected cost; cost decomposition; counterfactual interpretation; transaction-cost analysis.

## Part II - Learning from execution data

This part develops the research judgment needed to turn market observations into defensible measurements, models, and forecasts.

### 4 [Statistical Modeling as a Research Process](chapters/04-statistical-modeling.qmd#ch-modeling-research) {#plan-4 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Explains how to move from an observed market phenomenon to a model that can support an explanation, forecast, or decision. **Subtopics.** Research-question formation; the phenomenon, population, observational unit, target, and estimand; data-generating stories; prediction, explanation, causal estimation, and control; information available at decision time; data contracts; noisy labels; feature mechanisms and invariances; validation design; model ladders; bias, variance, and irreducible noise; learning curves; residual analysis; uncertainty; extrapolation; distribution shift; decision-aware evaluation; research logs and synthetic experiments.

### 5 [Execution Data: From Market Events to Research Tables](chapters/05-execution-data.qmd#ch-execution-data) {#plan-5 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Shows how orders, fills, quotes, and trades become a trustworthy research dataset without losing their timing or economic meaning. **Subtopics.** Order, fill, quote, trade, and depth records; entity keys and order lifecycles; sequence numbers and book replay; parent-order reconstruction; event alignment and latency-aware quote matching; timestamps and clock synchronization; calendar, event, and volume-time sampling; stale observations; missingness; cancellations and censored fills; corporate actions and effective-dated reference data; futures rolls and exact contract identity; live versus corrected data; leakage-safe joins; data lineage, reconciliation, and reproducible research tables.

### 6 [The Empirical Shape of Market Impact](chapters/06-empirical-market-impact.qmd#ch-impact-empirical) {#plan-6 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Describes the regularities seen in execution data before imposing a particular functional form or causal interpretation. **Subtopics.** Signed response and the missing no-trade path; child-order and parent-order scales; clock and quantity-progress trajectories; order size, intended and realized participation, and duration; concavity and square-root behavior; average, total, and marginal cost; temporary, transient, and permanent horizons; pauses, resilience, and post-trade decay; mechanical and informational response; volatility, spread, depth, and volume normalization; time-of-day effects; regimes and cross-sectional collapse; equities, futures, options, and less-liquid products; futures rolls; exploratory surface diagnostics; translation from empirical regularity to control input.

### 7 [Estimating Market Impact](chapters/07-estimating-market-impact.qmd#ch-impact-estimation) {#plan-7 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Develops statistical methods for estimating impact while being explicit about selection, endogeneity, uncertainty, and model use. **Subtopics.** Parametric and nonparametric specifications; log-log models; nonlinear and constrained regression; heteroskedasticity and heavy tails; hierarchical shrinkage; interactions and segmentation; metaorder reconstruction; endogenous participation and duration; latent urgency; confounding and selection; measurement error; causal designs; uncertainty intervals; stability; residual diagnostics; policy sensitivity.

### 8 [Short-Horizon Forecasting and Liquidity State](chapters/08-liquidity-state.qmd#ch-liquidity-state) {#plan-8 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Forecasts the market quantities that distinguish execution actions, including both liquidity conditions and short-lived price pressure. **Subtopics.** Decision horizons and action-conditional forecasts; intraday and remaining-day volume distributions; intended and realized participation; spread and depth transitions; book-walking cost; realized and forecast volatility; inventory-weighted forecast loss; imbalance, microprice, and order-flow imbalance; multi-horizon price and markout prediction; alpha decay and value net of execution cost; fill probability and fill-conditioned adverse selection; event intensities and point processes; state-space and latent-liquidity models; regime switching; trees, boosting, neural networks, and Gaussian processes; joint probabilistic forecasts; calibration; scenario generation; temporal leakage; forecast value for control; drift and fallback.

## Part III - From estimated models to execution policies

The emphasis now moves from describing costs and market state to choosing actions and understanding why an optimal policy behaves as it does.

### 9 Classical Optimal Liquidation {#plan-9 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Source draft** ]{.box}
:::

Derives the basic cost-risk trade-off and uses it to explain the shape of an optimal liquidation schedule. **Subtopics.** Discrete and continuous inventory dynamics; temporary impact; price risk; Bertsimas-Lo; Almgren-Chriss; expected cost and variance; the execution frontier; risk aversion and urgency; boundary conditions; closed-form trajectories; calibration; units and limiting cases; when the classical assumptions fail.

### 10 Volume Time, VWAP, and Participation Strategies {#plan-10 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Source draft** ]{.box}
:::

Connects optimal liquidation to the schedules and constraints used by practical execution algorithms. **Subtopics.** Calendar time and volume time; TWAP and VWAP schedules; constant and time-varying POV; uncertain future volume; participation caps and floors; completion constraints; catch-up logic near deadlines; benchmark-aware control; realized versus intended participation; interaction among impact, volume forecasts, and alpha decay.

### 11 Transient Impact and Market Resilience {#plan-11 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Introduces impact with memory and studies how liquidity recovery changes the value of waiting and the shape of a schedule. **Subtopics.** Propagator states; exponential and power-law kernels; resilience; path-dependent execution cost; child-order spacing; post-trade decay; kernel estimation; mechanical decay versus informational reversion; price manipulation; no-dynamic-arbitrage restrictions; optimal schedules under transient impact.

### 12 Adaptive Execution {#plan-12 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Explains how a policy should respond when forecasts, market conditions, or beliefs change during an order. **Subtopics.** Feedback policies; state and belief updates; receding-horizon control; model-predictive control; Bayesian learning; uncertain parameters; robust and distributionally robust optimization; dual control; changing volume, volatility, spread, and alpha; stability; excessive switching; hysteresis; guardrails; emergency completion; value of adaptation.

### 13 Passive Execution and Queue Control {#plan-13 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Values a resting order as a contingent execution whose apparent spread saving must be balanced against non-fill and adverse-selection risk. **Subtopics.** Posting versus crossing; queue priority and position; fill probability; queue depletion; cancellation and reposting; conditional markouts; adverse selection after fills; survival and hazard models; marked point processes; non-fill and deadline risk; impulse control; aggressiveness selection.

### 14 Routing, Dark Liquidity, and Auctions {#plan-14 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Extends the action from trading speed to venue, order type, and trading mechanism. **Subtopics.** Fragmented liquidity; fees and rebates; latency; fill quality; venue-specific toxicity; dark pools and conditional liquidity; information leakage; price protection; contextual bandits; constrained routing; opening and closing auctions; imbalance information; crossing opportunities; joint control of schedule, aggressiveness, and venue.

### 15 Futures Execution {#plan-15 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Treats contract choice, roll dynamics, and economic exposure as part of the execution decision rather than as data-cleaning details. **Subtopics.** Contract multipliers, tick sizes, and risk-equivalent quantity; margin versus exposure; contract liquidity measures; front and deferred contracts; liquidity migration; roll timing; basis and calendar spreads; outright versus spread execution; continuous-series distortions; session boundaries; expiry effects; roll-aware impact models; two-expiry control; underestimation near rolls.

## Part IV - Determining whether a policy works

A policy must be evaluated as a policy. These chapters separate genuine improvement from changes in order mix, market conditions, or the algorithm’s own selection behavior.

### 16 [Experiments and Policy Evaluation](chapters/16-policy-evaluation.qmd#ch-policy-evaluation) {#plan-16 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Develops credible ways to decide whether a new execution policy improves outcomes and for which orders it improves them. **Subtopics.** Randomized execution experiments; A/B tests and switchbacks; stratification; interference; selection into algorithms; completion bias and censoring; common support; counterfactual policy values; inverse-propensity weighting; doubly robust estimation; heterogeneous effects; uncertainty for policy differences; economic versus statistical significance; staged rollout and monitoring.

### 17 Reinforcement Learning for Execution {#plan-17 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Examines when execution should be treated as a learned sequential policy and why offline data make that problem difficult. **Subtopics.** MDPs and partially observed MDPs; state, action, transition, and reward design; inventory and deadline constraints; simulator construction; simulator bias; behavior policies; offline reinforcement learning; off-policy evaluation; distribution shift; conservative policy improvement; safe exploration; policy guardrails; comparison with model-predictive control.

## Part V - Other trading problems through the control lens

The same language of state, belief, action, cost, and feedback is applied to other central problems in algorithmic trading.

### 18 Market Making and Inventory Control {#plan-18 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Studies bid and ask decisions when the trader earns spread but accumulates inventory and adverse-selection risk. **Subtopics.** Reservation prices; Avellaneda-Stoikov; inventory penalties; quote skew; order-arrival calibration; fill probabilities; adverse selection; queue-aware quoting; volatility and regime changes; latency; multi-asset inventory; practical limits of stylized models.

### 19 Multi-Asset and Portfolio Execution {#plan-19 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Coordinates the liquidation of related positions when risk, liquidity, and impact are coupled across instruments. **Subtopics.** Basket execution; covariance and factor risk; factor liquidity; cross-impact; coupled schedules; hedging during execution; index rebalances; portfolio transitions; manipulation-free cross-impact; parameter estimation; robustness to unstable correlations and liquidity.

### 20 Portfolio Choice with Trading Frictions {#plan-20 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Connects forecasts and desired positions to the costly, gradual process of moving an actual portfolio. **Subtopics.** Signals and expected returns; turnover; transaction costs; signal decay; dynamic mean-variance control; no-trade regions; impulse and singular control; model-predictive rebalancing; robust portfolios; execution-aware portfolio construction; the boundary between portfolio and execution decisions.

### 21 Optimal Stopping and Statistical Arbitrage {#plan-21 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Develops entry, exit, and abandonment decisions when waiting changes both information and opportunity. **Subtopics.** Stopping times; continuation value; Snell envelopes and dynamic programming; free-boundary intuition; mean-reverting spreads; pairs and relative-value models; regime uncertainty; sequential testing; transaction costs; delayed execution; signal decay; when a statistically attractive trade is not economically worth taking.

### 22 Options Hedging under Frictions {#plan-22 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Studies hedging when rebalancing is discrete, costly, and itself moves the market. **Subtopics.** Delta and gamma exposure; discrete hedging error; stochastic volatility; transaction costs; impact-aware rebalancing; inventory constraints; no-trade regions; volatility and jump risk; joint hedge and execution decisions; liquidity differences across strikes and maturities.

### 23 Strategic Traders and Stochastic Games {#plan-23 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Explains when market response depends on the beliefs and actions of other strategic participants, not only on exogenous noise. **Subtopics.** Signaling through order flow; strategic liquidation; predatory trading; information leakage; equilibrium impact; best responses; stochastic differential games; mean-field games; competition among execution algorithms; mechanism design; limits of single-agent control models.

## Part VI - Conducting execution research

The final part brings the statistical, economic, and control ideas together in complete research workflows.

### 24 [From Research Question to Production Model](chapters/24-production-research.qmd#ch-production-research) {#plan-24 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **First draft** ]{.box}
:::

Follows a model from its first research question through deployment, monitoring, and communication with traders and engineers. **Subtopics.** Problem statements and decision context; simple benchmarks; exploratory analysis; preregistered validation; reproducible experiments; feature and model versioning; leakage controls; stress and sensitivity tests; translating estimates into policy behavior; model-engine interfaces; monitoring and drift; retraining; governance; rollback; communicating uncertainty.

### 25 Worked Research Studies {#plan-25 .unnumbered}

::: roadmap-status
[ **Planned** ]{.box}
:::

Presents complete investigations so the reader can see how the book’s principles interact when the data and conclusions are imperfect. **Subtopics.** Estimating an equity impact curve; diagnosing time-of-day effects; estimating transient-impact decay; designing and evaluating adaptive POV; modeling passive fills and adverse selection; futures execution around a roll; reproducing Almgren-Chriss and a propagator model; comparing a learned policy with a controlled baseline.

**Appendices.** Probability and conditional expectation; martingales and stopping times; Brownian motion, Itô calculus, and jump processes; dynamic programming, HJB equations, and verification; convex optimization, KKT conditions, and numerical control; statistical inference, regularization, and causal estimation; time-series and event-data methods; notation, units, and dimensional analysis.
